overview: These map labels span several phases: Bulgars on the Black Sea steppe, a Danube state formed among Slavic and other communities, and medieval Bulgarian kingdoms. They do not describe one unchanging population. Volga Bulgaria followed a separate history. Later Balkan art and books belong to the explicitly dated periods below.

periods.title: Steppe background
periods.summary: Kubrat's Bulgar confederation broke apart under Khazar pressure; different groups followed different routes.

periods.title: First Bulgarian state
periods.summary: The Danube state developed Christian institutions and important centres of art and writing before Byzantine conquest in 1018.

periods.title: Byzantine rule
periods.summary: The independent first kingdom had ended. A continuous Bulgarian polygon during this interval should not be read as continuous sovereignty.

periods.title: Second Bulgarian kingdom
periods.summary: Revolt restored Bulgarian rule in the 1180s. Later rulers supported the Tarnovo artistic and literary world before Ottoman conquest.

items.text: The early-eighth-century Madara Rider shows a horseman above a fallen lion on a high rock face. Its setting made a ruler's image part of the landscape. It is a royal monument, not evidence that villagers routinely went lion hunting.

Inscriptions beside the rider record events associated with rulers including Tervel and Omurtag. Text and image together provide evidence for early Bulgarian political memory; the cliff is more than a giant picture frame.

Boris I's adoption of Christianity in the 860s transformed official religious institutions. It did not instantly replace every household practice or erase the older histories of the people living in the state.

Early Bulgar cemeteries at Balchik, Novi Pazar, Kyulevcha and Topola contained ceramic jugs, bowls and other table vessels. Scholars compare their shapes with metal, glass and wooden examples from wider Eurasian traditions. Similar shape alone does not prove a pot was imported.

Four pottery kilns at the early medieval settlement of Topola demonstrate production, not just consumption. The study associates these vessel traditions especially with the first half and middle of the 700s. Someone had to make the dishes before anyone could argue about washing them.

Preslav excavations recovered agricultural and craft tools alongside pots, cups, bowls and amphoras. These ordinary objects connect the capital to food production and skilled work, rather than only to the activities of its rulers.

The Preslav museum distinguishes locally produced pottery from vessels imported from Byzantium. A household could use objects with different production histories; an imported container does not by itself tell us who lived in the house.

Earrings, bracelets and rings at Preslav include copper, bronze and silver examples, with glass, amber and other materials also represented. Dressing up had a much wider material range than gold treasure alone suggests.

A gold ring found at Pliska has a split and thinned ends that may reflect resizing. Its human portrait cannot be securely named. The wear and adjustments suggest an object with a history of use, not simply an untouched badge of a famous king.

At Patleina near Preslav, excavations in 1909 found fragments of a tenth-century ceramic portrait of St Theodore. Its large face was assembled from square tiles about 12 centimetres across: a carefully planned image made from separate fired pieces.

Monastic workshops around Preslav made painted tiles for churches and palaces. The saint portrait uses dark outlines, coloured slips and glaze. Archaeological workshop discoveries support local production, rather than assuming that every impressive object came from Byzantium.

Early Bulgarian inscriptions describe elite gifts and feasting. A recent study interprets these occasions as ways to display rank and strengthen personal ties. Royal hospitality was political work; it is not a menu for the average family.

In 1355-1356 the monk Simeon copied a lavish Gospel book for Tsar Ivan Alexander. Its parchment pages carry Slavonic text in Cyrillic. The manuscript's named scribe gives us a specific person behind the broad label “medieval learning.”

The same book uses gold for chapter titles in its margins and red for directions used in worship. Colour helped readers navigate the text. These are features of an expensive royal commission, not evidence that every household owned illustrated books.

A royal family portrait opens the Gospel book, while a word puzzle on folio 273v encodes Ivan Alexander's name. A medieval book could combine sacred reading, family image-making and an elaborate puzzle.

Κανα συβιγι Ωμουρταγ is the ruler's title and name, conventionally rendered “Kan sybigi Omurtag.” It begins a ninth-century Greek funerary inscription for Turdatzis on limestone. The sample follows the scholarly transcription, joining a line break. The title is Bulgar vocabulary written in Greek letters, not modern Bulgarian.

The inscriptions studied by Matilde Casas Olea preserve forms of ninth-century everyday Greek rather than only polished literary language. They show how Bulgarian rulers used a neighbouring written language in their new Balkan setting.

ending.text: Byzantine conquest ended the first Bulgarian kingdom in 1018. Renewed Bulgarian rule emerged in the 1180s, and Ottoman conquest ended the later medieval kingdoms in the late 1300s. Bulgarian communities, religious life and literary traditions continued. Neither the map's 1000 change of label nor its 1400 boundary is a disappearance of a people.
